title: Electrostatics: charges, forces and electric fields
voiceInstructions: Warm, engaging female teacher with a natural General American English accent. Relaxed, welcoming and lightly playful, with a gentle smile and conversational rhythm. Keep scientific terms precise and avoid an announcer cadence. Slow down for equations, numbers and conversions. Give brief natural thinking pauses after questions. Do not add words or laughter absent from the script.

sources.title: NTA: Official JEE Main 2026 syllabus, Physics Unit 11

chapters.title: Charge is transferred, not invented
chapters.formula: Q = n e; e approximately 1.60 x 10^-19 C; total charge conserved
points: An isolated system conserves its total electric charge.
Ordinary macroscopic charge transfer involves electrons; neutral means equal positive and negative charge.
Charge is additive algebraically, and ordinary isolated-body charge is quantized.
chapters.script: Hey, welcome back. Rub a balloon and it can attract tiny pieces of paper. Something invisible has changed, but we haven't created a new kind of matter. We have transferred electric charge. There are positive and negative charges. A neutral body contains both, with equal total amounts, so its net charge is zero. In ordinary rubbing and charging of solids, electrons are transferred between materials; the positively charged atomic nuclei do not usually travel from one object to another. If a body loses electrons, its net charge becomes positive. If it gains electrons, it becomes negative. The total charge of an isolated system is conserved. Charge adds algebraically, so plus three microcoulombs and minus five microcoulombs give minus two microcoulombs overall. A microcoulomb is one millionth of a coulomb. Ordinary isolated-body charge comes in integer multiples of the elementary charge, approximately one point six times ten to the minus nineteen coulombs. If a body gains ten trillion electrons, its charge change is minus one point six microcoulombs. Don't lose that minus sign. Attraction of neutral paper doesn't prove that the paper had an opposite net charge beforehand. Its charges can rearrange, creating polarization. Conductors allow mobile charges to redistribute; insulators restrict their motion. For JEE, separate charge transfer, net charge and polarization before deciding what an observation really tells you.

chapters.title: Coulomb's law: magnitude first, direction next
chapters.formula: F = k |q1 q2|/r^2; k approximately 9.0 x 10^9 N m^2/C^2 in vacuum
points: Use Coulomb's law for stationary point charges, or suitable point-charge approximations.
Like charges repel and unlike charges attract along the line joining them.
Doubling separation divides force magnitude by four.
chapters.script: Let's put two stationary point charges in vacuum. Coulomb's law says the force magnitude is proportional to the product of their charge magnitudes and inversely proportional to the square of their separation. The constant is approximately nine billion in SI units. The line joining the charges gives the force direction: like signs repel, opposite signs attract. Use the absolute charge product for magnitude, then decide direction from the signs and geometry. Suppose plus two microcoulombs and minus three microcoulombs are thirty centimeters apart. Convert the charges to coulombs and the distance to zero point three meters. The force magnitude is nine times ten to the ninth, times six times ten to the minus twelve, divided by zero point zero nine. That is zero point six newtons. On each charge, the force points toward the other. The forces have equal magnitudes and opposite directions, even if the charges or masses differ. Equal force does not require equal acceleration. Now double the separation. What happens? Give yourself a moment. The denominator becomes four times larger, so the force becomes zero point one five newtons. These are electrostatic point-charge results. Nearby extended charged conductors can redistribute charge, so don't blindly treat every object's entire charge as concentrated at its center. A uniform dielectric can change the interaction constant under the appropriate ideal model; our worked example uses vacuum.

chapters.title: Superposition means vector addition
chapters.formula: Fnet = sum of individual force vectors; add components, not just magnitudes
points: Calculate each source's force independently at the chosen target charge.
Choose axes and retain direction signs before adding components.
A zero net force at one point does not mean no individual forces act there.
chapters.script: Now add a third charge. Do we invent a new three-charge formula? No. For point charges at specified positions, calculate the force from each other charge independently, then add the force vectors. That's superposition. Always choose the target charge first. Otherwise it's surprisingly easy to add forces acting on different objects, which is not a valid net force calculation. Let's place a positive one microcoulomb target at the origin. A positive one microcoulomb source sits thirty centimeters to its right, and another equal positive source sits thirty centimeters above it. The right-hand source pushes the target left. The upper source pushes it downward. Each force magnitude is zero point one newtons. Therefore the x component is minus zero point one and the y component is minus zero point one newtons. The resultant magnitude is the square root of their squared sum, about zero point one four one newtons, directed diagonally down and left. Adding the two magnitudes to get zero point two would be wrong because the forces are perpendicular. If instead equal positive sources sit symmetrically on the left and right, their forces cancel at the center. Each individual force is still present. With unequal sources, write the signed component equation and solve; don't assume cancellation happens at the midpoint. In JEE, a small direction sketch before substitution can save a perfectly good numerical calculation from a wrong final answer.

chapters.title: Electric field describes what a charge would feel
chapters.formula: E = F/qtest; point source: E = k |Q|/r^2; force: F = q E
points: Field direction is the force direction for a positive test charge.
A negative test charge experiences force opposite to the field.
Fields add as vectors; field lines are a visualization, not particle trajectories.
chapters.script: Electric field lets us describe the influence of source charges before choosing the charge that will feel it. At a point, the field is force per unit positive test charge, with the test charge small enough not to disturb the source arrangement. Its unit is newtons per coulomb. For a point source, field magnitude is the Coulomb constant times the source charge magnitude divided by distance squared. Field points away from a positive source and toward a negative source. Notice that the field belongs to the source arrangement, not to the sign of the charge we later place there. A positive charge feels force along the field; a negative charge feels force opposite to it. At twenty centimeters from a positive two microcoulomb source in vacuum, field magnitude is four hundred and fifty thousand newtons per coulomb, directed outward. Place a negative one nanocoulomb test charge there. Its force magnitude is zero point zero zero zero four five newtons and its direction is inward. Field lines indicate the local field direction by their tangent. They do not cross where a unique nonzero field exists, and they are not automatically the paths moving particles follow. To combine several sources, add field vectors first, then multiply by the chosen test charge. Two equal opposite charges can produce a strong field between them even though their total net charge is zero. Total charge alone doesn't determine the field at every point.

chapters.title: A dipole can rotate without a net force
chapters.formula: p = q d, from negative to positive; torque = p E sin(theta) in a uniform field
points: An electric dipole has equal opposite charges separated by a distance d.
A uniform external field produces zero net force but can produce torque.
Far from a dipole: axial field magnitude approximately 2kp/r^3; equatorial approximately kp/r^3.
chapters.script: Take equal positive and negative charges separated by distance d. Together they form an electric dipole. Its dipole moment has magnitude q times the full separation, and its direction is from the negative charge to the positive charge. In a uniform external field, the positive charge feels a force along the field while the negative charge feels an equal force opposite to it. Net force is zero, but if the dipole is tilted these forces act along different lines. They create a torque. Its magnitude is dipole moment times field times sine of the angle between them, and the vector form is p cross E. The torque tends to align the dipole with the field. For charges of two nanocoulombs separated by one centimeter, dipole moment is two times ten to the minus eleven coulomb meters. In a uniform field of one hundred thousand newtons per coulomb at thirty degrees, torque is one times ten to the minus six newton meters. Both aligned and opposite alignment give zero torque, but aligned orientation is stable and opposite alignment is unstable. Zero torque alone doesn't prove stability. Far from the dipole compared with its separation, its axial field magnitude is approximately twice k p divided by r cubed, while the equatorial magnitude is k p divided by r cubed and points opposite to p. Those are far-field approximations, not exact formulas close to a charge. A nonuniform external field can also give a dipole a net force. Next we'll build on these field ideas with flux and Gauss's law.

quiz.question: A neutral body gains 10^13 electrons. Using e = 1.60 x 10^-19 C, its net charge becomes:
quiz.explanation: Electron transfer gives Q = -Ne = -1.6 x 10^-6 C.

quiz.question: Charges +2 microC and -3 microC are 0.30 m apart in vacuum. Using k = 9 x 10^9, force magnitude is:
quiz.explanation: F = 9 x 10^9 x 6 x 10^-12 / 0.09 = 0.6 N. The force is attractive.

quiz.question: Two perpendicular force components on one charge are -0.1 N each. Net force magnitude is approximately:
A field points right with magnitude 4.5 x 10^5 N/C. Force on -1 nanoC is:
quiz.explanation: F = qE. A negative charge reverses direction; magnitude = 10^-9 x 4.5 x 10^5 = 4.5 x 10^-4 N.

quiz.question: A dipole has charges of magnitude 2 nanoC separated by 0.01 m. In uniform E = 10^5 N/C at 30 degrees, torque magnitude is:
quiz.explanation: p = 2 x 10^-11 C m; torque = pE sin(30 degrees) = 10^-6 N m.
